name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Notwithstanding Mayor Wu’s claims, the ‘State of the Schools’ in Boston is not good
text:
THE REALITY OF public education in Boston is far from what Mayor Michelle Wu depicted in her recent State of the Schools address. Hiding behind the improvements she touted is a broken system with abysmal performance outcomes across every grade in the district. 
In the Boston Public Schools, seven out of every 10 third-graders can’t read or do math at grade level, which is also true for eighth-graders. The outcomes are far worse for Black and Latino students, multilingual learners, students with disabilities, and low-income students in Grades 3-8, with proficiency levels as low as 4 percent for some subgroups. 
It serves no benefit to students and families to push this truth aside or to dismiss this data point as “one number.” Our city must do better, and the first step to real improvement is acknowledging this grim reality, something Mayor Wu continues to fail to do.  
When asked head-on about these low performance outcomes, the mayor stumbled, citing “accountability metrics in the speech.” But the metrics she shared hardly show any accountability at all and fail to address the real issue: that the vast majority of the 44,000 students in BPS can’t read or do math at grade level.  
In the wake of the recent Next Chapter Boston education advocacy campaign, Mayor Wu called the group’s billboards “cynical” and “disgusting.” The billboards show a picture of a child’s eyes with the phrase “BPS IS FAILING HER,” while citing the factual data that shows why.  After the ads were pulled from the MBTA, despite prior approval, it’s clear our city’s leaders are too fearful to come to terms with the truth.  
If anything, Mayor Wu’s education speech should be described as cynical, pointing to misleading numbers and increased investment in a handful of student clubs, instead of the systemic academic overhauls that are required for improvement. In one year, the mayor announced, BPS went from six math clubs to 22 (out of 104 schools) at a time when only 33 percent of 10th-graders are doing math on grade level. For English learners, this number drops to 10 percent, and for students with disabilities it is 6 percent. 
Mayor Wu mentioned that BPS had their highest graduation rate last year, but seniors at BPS need only a D- to prove “competency” and pass core courses. Meanwhile, without MCAS as a graduation requirement, is a BPS diploma worth what it claims with standards set so low? 
The mayor also noted that Boston’s third-grade reading scores have ranked at the top of its urban school district cohort for each of the past six years. But this is disingenuous framing that makes it appear as if reading scores are actually good.  
In reality, just 29 percent of BPS students in grades 3-8 met state proficiency in reading and math on the 2026 MCAS, compared with the statewide average of 40 percent — itself a worrisome statistic.  
Our state leaders, who consistently cheerlead about Massachusetts’s number one national ranking, also need to come clean about the crisis in education that we’re experiencing. The ranking that really needs their focus is that the Commonwealth also holds the distinction of having some of the largest achievement gaps in the country. 
BPS uses its own Focus early literacy curriculum, which has been in place for more than 10 years with little results. Teachers and school administrators have voiced concerns about this curriculum and have seen no change from the district.  
The mayor spent a significant amount of time in her speech celebrating the expansion of free weekend sports, opening vocational programs at Madison Park to the community,  and expanding early college. These “nice-to-have” additions are not what BPS should be focusing on given its true state of crisis. We need real academic overhauls, acceleration academies on school breaks, and ongoing data sharing and dissemination practices to set real benchmarks for improvements across every grade.   
To continue to pretend like our schools are better than they really are is a disservice to students, teachers, families, and the city at large. The same is true of painting a picture of widespread progress when not nearly enough is being done to address our deep-rooted issues.  
The mayor also promised to set five-year targets that will improve poor performances, like attendance rates and test scores. These goals are meaningless if they don’t include concrete, measurable benchmarks. The updated 2026-2031 Strategic Roadmap for BPS, introduced at the beginning of this academic year, reads more like a roadblock. It’s vague and neglects to establish real plans or standards for needed growth.  
With years to create this plan, why are district leaders overlooking such essential details? We need to set real, achievable targets for improvements across all grades in reading, writing, math, and science, and develop a step-by-step implementation strategy to do this. 
These can’t be goals that keep getting pushed back to far-future dates. We have to create policies that make change for students now, so our city can live up to the true promise of delivering a quality public education to all students.  
With a total budget of $1.7 billion, per-pupil spending in Boston is among the highest in the nation, at roughly $37,000 per student. With such deep pockets, you would think it would be easier to integrate a concrete plan for improvement in literacy and numeracy among students. The question is not whether we invest enough money in our schools, but whether we are putting this money in the right places to achieve better results versus paying for the same mistakes year after year. 
The challenges BPS faces, whether they are academic or operational, are compounding. From literacy and math scores to chronic absenteeism to a $200 million transportation system that seems incapable of delivering students to school on time, all performance indicators are either stagnant or moving in the wrong direction.  The “fix” requires both immediate interventions and long-term policy shifts.  
This starts with true oversight and accountability standards that directly tie district funding to verifiable student benchmarks, operational efficiencies, and a guarantee that all students are safe within their school environments. Today, none of these three critical levers for change are evident.  
If the mayor is truly committed to making BPS the “best in the nation,” she and other city leaders must come to terms with the fact that we cannot achieve this without first recognizing where we are drastically falling short. And despite what Mayor Wu has stated publicly, this campaign is not aimed at families, students, or teachers; it is aimed at the people who have the power to change this. 
Mary Tamer, a former member of the Boston School Committee, is the executive director of MassPotential, a fiscally sponsored program of the Goodnation Foundation. Next Chapter Boston is an initiative of MassPotential. Vernée Wilkinson is the director of the Family Advisory Board at SchoolFacts Boston, a nonprofit working to improve education for all in Boston.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Canyon County judge declines to halt pro-Prop 1 ballot initiative ads amid lawsuit
text:
Volunteers pass boxes of signatures supporting a ballot initiative to end Idaho's strict ban on abortion on July 2, 2026, outside the state Capitol in Boise. (Photo by Abigail Gerstein/Idaho Capital Sun)This story was first published by Boise State Public Radio on Oct. 30, 2026.
A Canyon County judge has rejected a request by anti-Proposition 1 campaigners to halt TV ads from airing that promote the ballot measure days before the election.
In an opinion released late Friday night, Judge Davis VanderVelde found the ads did not violate Idaho campaign finance laws and declined to keep them from being broadcast by local stations.
A Republican Party operative and three board members of Too Extreme for Idaho, which opposes restoring abortion rights under Prop 1, filed their lawsuit Tuesday morning.
They said the scheme used by Idahoans United for Women and Families (IUWF), the Idaho Democratic Party and its gubernatorial candidate, Terri Pickens, concealed the true origin of who paid for the ads.
IUWF, which qualified Prop 1 for the ballot, gave the Idaho Democratic Party more than $720,000 in recent weeks. The party then purchased advertising through Pickens’ campaign.
All political candidates receive significant discounts on ads in the 60 days leading up to an election compared to political groups.
“Ultimately, Plaintiffs’ assertion that the monies from IUWF were specifically contributed for support of Proposition 1 with the intent of concealing the original donor for such advertisements requires logical leaps that are not fully supported by the evidence,” VanderVelde wrote.
Each of these transactions is publicly available in the state’s campaign finance database, which the plaintiffs cited in the evidence presented to the judge.
VanderVelde said there’s also no evidence showing that IUWF still controlled the hundreds of thousands of dollars it donated to the state Democratic Party.
An attorney for the defendants argued in court Thursday that the party had the final say in how any of that money was spent, which VanderVelde said was not proven otherwise by the plaintiffs.
“The Court recognizes that the parties have had a short time to advance this lawsuit and that if there was additional time, additional facts may be developed by either party which could lend further credence to their claims or defenses,” he wrote.
That said, the judge found there may still be outstanding legal questions about whether the ads are truly for a candidate or a proposition and whether the lower rates should apply.
“However, without further law or authority significant questions remain as to what constitutes an appropriate advertisement under the law in order to qualify as an advertisement promoting a candidate.”
Tom Luna, one of the plaintiffs, released a statement saying he and the three other men who brought the lawsuit disagree with the decision, but that it was important voters know who paid for the ads.
“I’m sure many voters are as mad as I am about these dirty tricks. Let’s make sure we turn our frustration into action by showing up on Election Day, making our voices heard, and standing for life,” Luna said.
A request for comment from the Idaho Democratic Party wasn’t immediately returned late Friday night.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: New Oklahoma laws take effect on Sunday
text:
An adult Carolina mantis is pictured on a plant. Oklahoma lawmakers have made the Carolina mantis the state predator insect. (Photo by Grandbrothers/Getty Images)OKLAHOMA CITY – More than 200 new laws take effect Sunday following a legislative session that ended in May.
Oklahoma’s newest laws run the gamut from ones designed to protect children to requiring GPS monitoring for some domestic violence defendants to new state symbols.
Here’s a few of them: 
Ban on all childhood marriage 
Senate Bill 504 sets the marital age at 18.
The measure repeals all exceptions for minors getting married, including allowing matrimony with parental permission or with a court’s permission. Existing law allowed children 16 or under to be married with a judge’s permission.
The measure passed the state House by a single vote.
“It is one more thing we can do to protect children from predators,” said Sen. Warren Hamilton, R-McCurtain.
Sen. Warren Hamilton, R-McCurtain, listens to the governor’s State of the State Address on Feb. 3, 2025, in the House chamber of the state Capitol. (Photo by Kyle Phillips/For Oklahoma Voice)
He said the measure will help preserve the dignity of marriage.
“Marriage is the biggest decision a lot of people will make,” Hamilton said.
Oklahoma becomes the 17th state to ban child marriage. 
Visitation changes
Senate Bill 2170 adds sexual abuse to the list of reasons why supervised visitation shall be required.
Under the new law, anyone who has had
substantiated findings by the Department of Human Services of  of sexualabuse of a child will be required to have a third party present when having visitation with a child.
New state symbols
Some new laws add to the state’s growing list of symbols.
Senate Bill 2159 designates wheat as the state crop.
Meanwhile, Senate Bill 2065, dubbed the “Lucile Morehouse Pollinator Act,” designates the European honeybee as the agricultural pollinator, the American bumblebee the native insect, the Carolina mantis as the predator insect, and the rainbow scarab, a dung beetle, as the soil conservation insect.
Morehouse and her mother started the Lucile’s Pollinator Project after learning that pollinators were in decline. The project provides free seeds.
Weakening the governor’s appointment powers 
Senate Bill 1327 restores the Oklahoma Tourism and Recreation Commission’s power to appoint the head of the Oklahoma Department of Tourism and Recreation.
It removes the governor’s power to make the appointment.
The action comes after the agency was embroiled in a scandal in which a restaurant vendor was convicted of defrauding the state of millions by submitting inflated invoices.
The agency head will serve at the pleasure of the commission instead of the governor, according to the measure.
Tracking domestic violence offenders
Senate Bill 1325 requires certain defendants charged with domestic violence offenses, who are released on bond, to wear a global positioning device that can be tracked by the victim.
Sen. Bill Coleman, R-Ponca City, is the author. Coleman said he talked to a number of judges who thought the measure could save lives.
Sen. Bill Coleman, R-Ponca City, sits at his desk on the Senate floor on May 21, 2025 ahead of the swearing in ceremony for a newly elected senator. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)
If a victim were able to have advance warning that the defendant was approaching their home or business, it would allow the victim to get to a safe location, Coleman said.
Marijuana packaging changes
House Bill 4454 prohibits edible marijuana packaging from being attractive to people under 18. It prohibits the use of cartoons, toys, animals and food to sell the product. It also bars the product from being shaped like commercially available candy.
Jed Green, director for Oklahomans for Responsible Cannabis Action, said laws like the one created by HB 4454 can be a little subjective.
“I would urge folks in the industry to err on the side of caution,” Green said. 
Rep. Carl Newton, R-Cherokee, said the measure also requires the products to list the content of Tetrahydrocannabinol, or THC, the psychoactive element of marijuana, to help prevent over medication.
Adoptions and gender-affirming care
House Bill 3586 prohibits the denial of adoption based on the parents’ refusal to enable the child to accessgender-affirming care.
Raising the child consistent with the child’s biological sex does not constitute abuse, according to the measure.
A new bridge
House Bill 2123 allows the Oklahoma Turnpike Authority to build a new bridge crossing the Arkansas River in the Bixby area.
Rep. Mark Tedford, R-Tulsa, said the measure empowers the agency to start surveying and evaluating locations for their portion of the project.
Rep. Mark Tedford, R-Tulsa, front, and Sen. Adam Pugh, R-Edmond, back, wait in line for candidate filing on April 1, 2026, at the state Capitol in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Additional roads would need to be built by local entities, he said.
“It is going to be a team effort to get the proper funding and get the whole project done,” Tedford said.
‘True Grit Trail’
House Bill 1411 establishes the True Grit Trail in southeast Oklahoma.
“True Grit” is a novel written by Arkansas-born author Charles Portis that depicts 14-year-old Mattie Ross’ efforts to avenge her father’s murder. It was made into a 1969 movie featuring the late John Wayne who plays U.S. Marshall Reuben J. “Rooster” Cogburn.
Much of the story was set in Oklahoma, said Rep. Jim Grego, R-Wilburton, in a statement.
“This new trail will give us a way to show off the places made popular in the story and  hopefully will draw new visitors to this area of the state,” Grego said. “This could positively impact our local hotels, restaurants and other businesses.”
Towns and places of interest along the trail include: Sallisaw, Spiro, Bokoshe, McCurtain, Kinta, Quinton, Krebs, McAlester, Hartshorne, Wilburton, Red Oak, Bengal, Talihina, Robbers Cave State Park and the Talimena National Scenic Byway.

name: California
title: Cómo la Proposición 45 podría alterar las luchas en California contra los centros de datos
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
Los votantes de California que estén considerando la Proposición 45 decidirán el destino de una medida de infraestructura de gran alcance que, según advierten sus opositores, podría dejar prácticamente sin efecto las nuevas leyes estatales sobre centros de datos.
 Eso facilitaría enormemente que los promotores inmobiliarios impongan instalaciones no deseadas en las comunidades locales, lo que podría socavar una creciente ola de prohibiciones, moratorias y resoluciones contra los centros de datos a nivel municipal y de condado.
 Los defensores de los centros de datos insisten en que la medida electoral no les reportará ningún beneficio, incluso cuando algunos beneficiarios de los centros de datos están invirtiendo grandes sumas de dinero para respaldar la Proposición 45.
 Los partidarios de la Proposición 45 la han presentado como una herramienta para acelerar proyectos de infraestructura crítica , como viviendas y escuelas, y la medida no menciona directamente los centros de datos entre los tipos de proyectos que considera críticos. Sin embargo, algunos expertos legales y defensores del medio ambiente afirman que el lenguaje técnico de la proposición crea una laguna legal. Al agilizar las evaluaciones ambientales bajo la Ley de Calidad Ambiental de California para amplias categorías de proyectos —incluidas las instalaciones de internet de banda ancha y cualquier infraestructura adicional necesaria para su funcionamiento—, la medida podría permitir discretamente que los centros de datos eludan las recientes salvaguardias estatales y el escrutinio local.
 Julia Stein, experta en derecho y subdirectora del Instituto Emmett sobre Cambio Climático y Medio Ambiente de la Facultad de Derecho de UCLA, advierte que la medida actúa como un “instrumento de fuerza bruta en lo que respecta a la racionalización” debido a la amplitud de su ámbito de aplicación secundario.
 “Lo que hace la Proposición 45 es designar toda una categoría de proyectos que estarían sujetos a una simplificación, y también establece que los proyectos auxiliares a esos proyectos —es decir, algo que podría ser necesario hacer durante el desarrollo del proyecto que está exento— quedarían incluidos en esa misma simplificación”, dijo Stein.
 Los proyectos de telecomunicaciones se simplifican explícitamente según la propuesta, “y hay argumentos para considerar que el desarrollo de centros de datos podría ser necesario para proyectos de ese tipo”, añadió Stein.
 Otros proyectos, como el tren de alta velocidad, quedan explícitamente excluidos de la simplificación de trámites según la propuesta, pero los centros de datos tampoco figuran en esa lista. Stein y otros tres expertos en derecho ambiental declararon a CalMatters que esto abre la puerta a posibles impugnaciones legales.
 “El hecho de que hayan excluido algunos proyectos, pero no hayan excluido expresamente los centros de datos, probablemente un tribunal lo interpretaría no como un descuido involuntario, sino más bien como una intención de incluir los centros de datos en la iniciativa”, dijo Matt McKerley, abogado de Shute, Mihaly y Weinberger.
 Además, los opositores argumentan que la redacción de la propuesta, que incluye una cláusula que establece que prevalecería sobre otras leyes relacionadas, anularía medidas como el Proyecto de Ley 887 del Senado , aprobado recientemente, que dificultó la tramitación acelerada de la revisión ambiental para los centros de datos.
 Los representantes del sector afirman que estas objeciones a la Proposición 45 son infundadas. La Coalición de Centros de Datos, un grupo industrial que apoya la Proposición 45, insiste en que sus instalaciones quedan fuera del alcance de la iniciativa, que se centra principalmente en el desarrollo de viviendas y otras infraestructuras como carreteras y puentes.
 “La Coalición de Centros de Datos ha revisado la Proposición 45 y ha llegado a la conclusión de que los centros de datos no cumplen los requisitos para la simplificación que contempla la Proposición 45, ni son una entidad cubierta por ninguna parte de la medida”, dijo Khara Boender, Directora de Asuntos Gubernamentales para la Región Oeste de la coalición.
 Los representantes del sector también hacen referencia a un reciente dictamen jurídico de la Oficina de Asesoría Legislativa de California, que presta servicios legales a los miembros de la Legislatura. El dictámenes argumenta que las definiciones legales de la Proposición 45 no se aplican a los centros de datos.
 Amelia Matier, de la campaña “Sí a la Proposición 45”, se hizo eco de esa opinión, afirmando: “Los centros de datos no están incluidos en la Proposición 45”. Añadió: “Los defensores del inasequible statu quo de California están desesperados por distraer a los votantes con mentiras porque no pueden justificar las costosas demoras y la burocracia que elevan los precios para las familias trabajadoras “ .
 Entre los opositores a la medida se encuentran la Federación Laboral de California, el Centro Occidental de Derecho y Pobreza, y varios grupos de defensa del medio ambiente que han gastado más de 31 millones de dólares para oponerse a la medida.
A pesar de sostener que los centros de datos quedan fuera del alcance de la propuesta, los intereses tecnológicos y de servicios públicos que se benefician del auge informático de California están impulsando su aprobación con un enorme apoyo financiero . Los defensores han invertido más de 40 millones de dólares en la campaña a favor de la Proposición 45, incluyendo 3.05 millones de dólares del gigante de servicios públicos PG&E y 500,000 dólares del desarrollador de almacenes y centros de datos Prologis; una inyección de capital que, según los opositores, revela quién espera realmente beneficiarse si la medida se aprueba.
 El debate sobre el impacto de la Proposición 45 en los centros de datos surge en un momento crucial del auge de la infraestructura de IA en California. El gobernador Gavin Newsom firmó recientemente siete leyes históricas sobre centros de datos destinadas a obligar a los operadores a revelar su consumo de agua, financiar sus propias mejoras de la red eléctrica y someterse a una evaluación ambiental.
 Sin embargo, las comunidades locales no esperan a que entren en vigor las regulaciones estatales. Ante el creciente temor a las subidas de tarifas, la sobrecarga de la red eléctrica y el agotamiento del agua, ha surgido una fuerte oposición ciudadana en toda California. Al menos 26 ciudades y condados han propuesto o aprobado moratorias, prohibiciones o límites estrictos destinados a frenar la construcción de centros de datos en sus comunidades.
 Nina Robertson, abogada adjunta de la oficina regional de Earthjustice en California, afirmó que la ambigüedad del texto de la papeleta electoral desencadenaría de inmediato batallas legales sobre la autoridad local para otorgar permisos.
 “¿Y quién va a asumir el coste de ese litigio?”, preguntó Robertson. “Serán los gobiernos locales”.

name: VTDigger
title: Tax the rich to spare the rest of us
text:
Dear Editor,
There is one single, fundamental issue underlying the election next week, and many people speak a partial truth about it: Our taxes are too high. Agreed; for most Vermonters, they are.  
But some people’s taxes are too low. The wealthiest among us have not paid their fair share to properly support our society in generations, if ever. Not in Vermont, and not in the U.S.  
According to data from the Vermont Department of Taxes, the number of Vermont income tax filers earning more than $300,000 in 2015 was 3,519, just under 1% of all taxpayers. By 2024, this fortunate group had grown to 9,788, constituting just over 2.5% of taxpayers. In 2015, they collectively paid 6.93% of their income to the state, and in 2024 they paid 6.73%. During that time, their collective income nearly tripled. 
By my calculation, if this wealthiest cohort paid just 2% more, that would be about half what it would take to render taxes on anyone earning under $100,000 unnecessary. If they paid 6.2% more, no one making under $150,000 would need to pay taxes. That’s about 90% of us.
Is anyone proposing to tax the rich so hard they worry about affording heat this winter? Or keeping their cars running? Or even taxing them enough that they might worry about affording a vacation? No, of course not. 
Why, then, is it fair to tax any Vermonters to the point that any of us must have such fears?

READ MORE

Let’s compromise and consider taxing the rich just enough so their increased payments let us lower everyone else’s taxes and relieve everyone of such fears. In the process, we would fund our schools, roads and social services to a level where all Vermonters can start to feel that we live in a healthy state where everyone shares in the work.
We should each pay, within our means, toward the well-being of Vermont and its people. There is obviously a deep unfairness in our system when hardworking people are taxed so hard that it hurts, while wealthy people are not. 
If you want change, don’t get distracted by the implementation details. We will only get the chance for change if we elect people willing to effect change. The wealthy and comfortable buy our land and our houses; they vacation here and, yes, many make tax-deductible contributions to the nonprofits trying to provide a safety net. The wealthy own the TV and radio stations and social media platforms. They fund political parties and pay for political ads that overwhelm our thinking with the drumbeat that we need to cut “our” high taxes and that we must forever keep finding ways to do less with less. 
If you’re eligible to vote but not sure you are registered, call your friendly town clerk and find out. It’s a miracle of Vermont law that you can register and vote even on Election Day — though your hardworking clerk will appreciate you not waiting that long. Don’t miss this chance to change the failing status quo.
Alan Turnbull
Craftsbury, Vt.

name: California
title: California can’t afford to keep Prop 13 loopholes open when billions of dollars are on the line
text:
Guest Commentary written by

John Kim
John Kim is the president and CEO of Catalyst California.


I have fond memories of growing up in the suburbs of Los Angeles in the 1970s. The weather felt perfect. Yes, there were hot days, but you could look forward to perfect summer nights. Public schools felt relatively new, which they were, and there were open spaces yet to be explored. 
Though there was a new danger every week on the news, I somehow felt safe tumbling around, untethered, in the back of my parents’ station wagon. 
The state’s transformation over the last 50 years has been mind boggling. You likely would have been laughed out of most rooms in the ‘70s for predicting that California would become the fourth-largest economy on earth, behind only the United States, China and Germany. 
Innovations forged here reshaped how the world works. And yet, state and local governments failed to keep up.
The population nearly doubled, but we did too little to house these new Californians. We made some gains in public schools after short-sighted disinvestment during the 1980s and ‘90s, but we still struggle with achievement gaps across race and class.
We set conditions for technological invention but do too little to mitigate an exploding wealth gap that would make the Gilded Age blush. And we’re nowhere near ready to manage an AI-driven economic transition, let alone the increasing severity and cadence of climate catastrophes. 
The favorite bogeyman, though, is bureaucratic intransigence, sometimes called one-party rule. But we should be clear the problem isn’t partisanship or a lack of imagination — it’s structural and goes back to the 1970s. 
Proposition 13 was sold in 1978 as a way to save grandma’s house from unpredictable property tax bills. It also became a permanent discount for wealthy, corporate property owners. 
Under the proposition, homeowners pay taxes based on market value when they bought their homes, rather than on current values. And that’s fine. But since Prop 13 passed, high-priced tax attorneys have leveraged loopholes in Prop. 13 to let commercial and industrial property owners avoid property reassessments and higher taxes when their property changes hands. 
The result: billions of dollars in lost tax revenue.
USC researchers recently estimated that as much as $25.1 billion more could be collected per year by state and local governments if California closes Prop. 13’s commercial and industrial loophole and those properties are assessed at their current fair-market values.
Think of all we could do with those resources if we told wealthy corporations, after 50 years, that the party’s over.
California is about to need every dollar it can raise. 
President Donald Trump’s signature legislation, dubbed the One Big Beautiful Bill, takes healthcare and food aid from working families and hands the money to the wealthiest Americans.
Roughly 2 million Californians will fall off Medi-Cal by 2028, and nearly half a million are now being shoved off CalFresh. The state now has to cover a deficit of more than $20 billion a year.
And again public school districts up and down the state are struggling with empty coffers and potential layoffs.
Often big wins get lost in a bureaucratic wilderness, and cynicism rises among voters who are legitimately hurting.
But when we focus, we can get it right — like when the state offered all 4-year-olds an extra year of education by adding transitional kindergarten to public schools. This is a concrete, visionary program that protects the pocketbooks of California families while increasing trust in government.  
Now the Legislature and next governor have a rare political window. They can refill the federal breach and create a version of government we all want and need. The goal is not to restore California to 1970, but to build what will get us to 2070.
Until they seize this chance, the whole state is like me as a kid in the back of that station wagon: No seat belt. No headrest. Nothing to hold on to. 
Just sliding around, bracing for whatever comes next.

name: California
title: How Prop 45 could reshape California’s fight over data centers
text:
In summary
Prop. 45, billed as a pro-housing development measure, may have the unintended consequence of making it easier to build data centers, opponents say.




California voters considering Proposition 45 will decide the fate of a sweeping infrastructure measure that opponents warn could render the state’s brand-new data center laws virtually toothless.
That would make it far easier for developers to force unwanted facilities into local communities, potentially undermining a growing wave of bans, moratoriums, and anti-data-center resolutions at the city and county level.
Data center backers insist the ballot measure will do nothing for them — even as some data center beneficiaries are spending big backing Prop. 45.
Supporters have framed Prop. 45 as a tool to accelerate critical infrastructure projects, like housing and schools and the measure does not directly name data centers among the sorts of projects it considers critical. But some legal scholars and environmental advocates say that the proposition’s technical language creates a loophole. By expediting environmental reviews under the California Environmental Quality Act for broad categories of projects — including broadband internet facilities and any additional infrastructure required to get them up and running — the measure could quietly allow data centers to bypass recent state safeguards and local scrutiny.
Julia Stein, a legal scholar and deputy director at UCLA School of Law’s Emmett Institute on Climate Change and the Environment, warns that the measure acts as a “blunt force instrument when it comes to streamlining” because of how wide its secondary umbrella extends.
“What Prop. 45 does is designate an entire class of projects that would be subject to streamlining, and then it also says that projects ancillary to those projects — so something that you might need to do in the course of the development of the project that’s exempted itself — would fall within that same streamlining bubble,” Stein said. 
Telecommunications projects are explicitly streamlined under the proposition, “and there’s an argument that the development of data centers might be necessary for projects like that,” Stein added.
Other projects, like high-speed rail, are explicitly excluded from streamlining under the proposition — but data centers are not on that list, either. Stein and three other environmental law scholars told CalMatters that this opens the door for legal challenges.
“The fact that they excluded some projects but have not expressly excluded data centers, a court would probably actually interpret that not as an unintentional oversight, but rather as intent to include data centers in the initiative,” said Matt McKerley, an attorney with Shute, Mihaly and Weinberger. 
Further, opponents argue that the proposition’s language, which includes a clause that it would supersede other related laws, would override measures like the recently-passed Senate Bill 887, which made it harder to fast-track environmental review for data centers.
Industry representatives say these objections to Prop. 45 are misplaced. The Data Center Coalition, an industry group supporting Prop. 45, insists their facilities fall outside the initiative’s scope, which focuses largely on housing development.
“The Data Center Coalition has reviewed Proposition 45 and concluded that data centers are not eligible for Prop. 45’s streamlining, nor are they a covered entity under any part of the measure,” said Khara Boender, the coalition’s Director of Government Affairs—West.
Industry representatives also point to a recent legal opinion memo from California’s Office of Legislative Counsel, which provides legal services to members of the Legislature. The memo argues that Prop. 45’s statutory definitions do not apply to data centers.
Despite maintaining that data centers fall outside the proposition’s reach, tech and utility interests benefiting from California’s computing boom are putting massive financial weight behind its passage. Corporate backers have poured over $10 million into the Yes on Prop. 45 campaign, including $3.05 million from utility giant PG&E and $500,000 from warehouse and data center developer Prologis — a cash influx that opponents argue reveals who truly expects to profit if the measure passes. 
The debate over Prop. 45’s data center impact comes at a pivotal moment in California’s AI infrastructure boom. Gov. Gavin Newsom recently signed seven landmark data center laws aimed at forcing operators to disclose water usage, pay for their own grid upgrades, and undergo environmental review.
Yet local communities aren’t waiting for state regulations to take effect. Amid rising fears of rate hikes, grid overload, and water depletion, grassroots opposition has erupted across California. At least 26 cities and counties have proposed or passed moratoriums, bans, or strict limits aimed to stop data center development in their communities.
Nina Robertson, a deputy managing attorney in Earthjustice’s California regional office, said the ambiguity written into the ballot text would trigger immediate legal battles over local permitting authority.
“And who’s going to bear the cost of that litigation?” Robertson asked. “It’s going to be the local governments.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT will pay you to beat New York in court. Almost no one can collect.
text:
Last July, Connecticut passed a law that reads like a dare. 
Public Act 25-172 promises a Connecticut resident who pays New York income tax on days worked at home in Connecticut a credit equal to 60 percent of the extra Connecticut tax that results when the state recalculates the credit it gave for that New York tax. 
The act also waives penalties and interest on the late Connecticut tax. It reaches back to tax years beginning in 2020.
The target is New York’s convenience-of-the-employer rule. One sentence of New York regulation says a nonresident’s days worked outside New York count as New York days unless the work was done out of state “of necessity, as distinguished from convenience.” New York’s 2006 guidance confines the rule to employees whose primary office is in New York and excuses a home day only when the home is a “bona fide employer office.” A Connecticut resident with a Manhattan employer who works Fridays in Fairfield pays New York tax on Friday.
To collect Connecticut’s 60 percent, the resident must do four things, and the act joins them with “and.” Pay the New York tax. Apply to New York for a refund and be denied. Appeal that denial to a court or tribunal. Obtain a final decision ordering New York to refund the tax.
On July 2, the Appellate Division, Third Department, the court that hears appeals from New York’s Tax Appeals Tribunal, ruled against Edward Zelinsky, a Connecticut resident and law professor who has been fighting this rule since his first Tribunal decision in 2001. The Tribunal had ruled against him in May 2025. The court found “no constitutional or other infirmity” in the rule, said the debate over remote work “remain[s] the province of the Legislature,” and saw “no basis to disturb the Tribunal’s determination sustaining the taxation.” The one road the act requires a resident to travel, denial, appeal, and a final win, was just closed again by the court at the end of it. As far as I can find, nobody has yet qualified for the credit, and after July no one is likely to.
There is a second problem, and it is Connecticut’s own. 
Since tax years beginning in 2019, Connecticut has had the same rule. Section 12-711 of the General Statutes counts as Connecticut income the pay of a nonresident for “days worked outside this state for such person’s convenience if such person’s state of domicile uses a similar test.” The Department of Revenue Services says plainly that for a New York resident working from home for a Connecticut employer, “Connecticut will apply the New York ‘convenience of the employer’ test.” 
Connecticut taxes New Yorkers at home in New York exactly as New York taxes Connecticut residents at home in Connecticut. The act pays Connecticut residents to attack, in New York’s courts, a rule Connecticut keeps on its own books.
What actually protects a Connecticut commuter is older and duller than the bounty. Section 12-704 gives residents a credit for income tax paid to another state, claimed on Schedule 2 of the CT-1040. The instructions to that form define qualifying income to include compensation “for personal services performed from a home office in Connecticut for an employer in a qualifying jurisdiction that applies a convenience of the employer test.” 
In plain terms: Connecticut already credits the New York tax on those Fridays. The credit is capped at the share of Connecticut tax that the New York income represents, and it cannot push Connecticut tax below what would be due if the New York income were left out, so a resident still pays the difference where New York’s tax runs higher. But the resident is not taxed twice on the same wage. The commuter who files Schedule 2 correctly and attaches the New York return, as Connecticut requires, is made whole to the extent Connecticut law allows, with no lawsuit.
If the General Assembly believes the convenience rule is unjust, it has two honest options. It can repeal Connecticut’s mirror of the rule, which would cost the state revenue from New Yorkers and would at least match its words to its conduct. Or it can pursue what no two of New York, New Jersey and Connecticut have ever signed: a reciprocal agreement. New Jersey’s only such agreement, with Pennsylvania, covers wages and nothing else. A bounty for winning a case the courts have now rejected three times is neither.
In the meantime, Connecticut residents with New York offices should do three things this filing season. Keep a day log; New York audits these. Ask the employer, in writing, whether the home office meets New York’s bona fide employer office test. And claim the Schedule 2 credit, with the New York return attached. The remedy is already in the instructions.
Myung Keon Kim is a certified public accountant licensed in New York whose practice prepares New York, New Jersey and Connecticut returns for individuals and small businesses.
